A shadow before the cross, the greater fulfilment after it

Real double fulfilments follow one pattern: a shadow in the Old Testament and the greater fulfilment after the cross, in Christ and his church. Scripture gives no case of both fulfilments coming after the cross.
One tribulation such as never was, nor ever shall be
Equal to it, or greater: either way it would break “nor ever shall be”.

Jesus said the tribulation would be such as has not been since the beginning of the world, nor ever will be. If nothing before it matches it and nothing after it will, it cannot happen twice; and he placed all these things in one generation.
Many now agree Matthew 24 was fulfilled in AD 70, but say it will be fulfilled again in our future. Can it be fulfilled twice?
Some accept that Jesus foretold the fall of Jerusalem, yet keep a future tribulation by saying the prophecy will be fulfilled a second time.
Scripture does have them: the son of David who builds God's house was Solomon first, then Christ, who builds his church.
The first is a shadow before the cross; the greater fulfilment comes after it, in Christ and the church. There is no case of both coming after the cross.
When the abomination stood in the holy place, those in Judea were to flee: “for then there will be great tribulation.” That flight happened once.
Verse 21 says nothing before the tribulation matched it and nothing after it ever will. A later one equal to it, or greater, would contradict Jesus.
All these things, beginning with the temple's fall, would happen within that generation, not across two.

Supporters of a double fulfilment point to prophecies with near and far horizons, such as Isaiah 7:14, and argue that the cosmic signs and the gathering of the elect (24:29-31) go beyond AD 70, so a greater fulfilment is still to come.

Matthew 24's tribulation was a single, unrepeatable event in Jesus' own generation. If we see that he foretold AD 70, we should not keep a second, future tribulation to protect a system we were taught.
Many who hold this reading still expect Christ's future bodily return and the final judgement, which they find in other texts (Acts 1:11; 1 Corinthians 15).
